|---|---|---|

| Sequence/order of shipment journey | Ordinal | Vertical ordering from top to bottom along the bars |

- "How do we decrease time of arrival"

raw_comment:
1.I notice that the supply chain delays have become more prevalent throughout the pandemic. Processes that would typically take around 59 days was now taking roughly three months. The pandemic slowed most businesses down, and now its beginning to seem like it was a permanent effect. 
2.I wonder how companies that rely on fast paced shipping plan to innovate their way past these heavy effects of the pandemic such as Amazon, and do these delays come as a result of people not working due to the Covid-19 Pandemic?
3. Longer these supplies take, jobs are at risk. People could get fired, and people could go into desperate states due to lack of supplies. Not many consumers are able to purchase what they need due to it being stranded in a warehouse in the middle of neverland; thus also affecting businesses due to lack of money flowing leading to them possibly closing down
4."Stuck at sea, my package never arrived to me!"

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?

I noticed that throughout the pandemic, I've seen that supply chain delays have been more common. Processes that used to take 59 days to complete were now taking three months. Most enterprises were slowed by the pandemic, which now appears to have a long-term consequence.

2. What do you wonder?

I'm curious as to how long it will take to resolve this issue and how company owners will go about finding answers. Port congestion is a common issue that will certainly worsen as time goes on.

3. How does this relate to you and your community?

This relates to me and my community because ordering shipments may now take considerably longer than normal, causing customers to miss out on important deadlines. Many of the resources I use on a daily basis and have seen sold in stores come from global trade via cargo ships. The efficiency of this mode of transportation is disrupted by major delays in the voyage duration of these ships.

4. What’s going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.

This graph shows how backed up the cargo ships are right now, as well as how long it would typically take to meet the deadlines.

Catchy headline: Global Trade Slows Down

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that it takes a longer time for a good from Indonesia today than previously. 
2. I wonder if this is due to the pandemic, which leads to people preferring to have their goods delivered to them rather than them going outside to get the goods themselves. I also wonder how long ago "previously" is being used to define in this graph? Was it right before the pandemic, or actually sometime at the very beginning? The graph doesn't make that very clear. 
3. Nowadays, our community orders more stuff online. My family goes out to stores and restaurants less and less and order more take out and online deliveries when we want to buy or eat stuff.  
4. A good headline for this article could be "Cargo Shipping Experiences More Delays and Why".

raw_comment: I noticed that compared to the typical 59 days for usual cargo transportation, in the present day it is almost a month longer for the same process we used to practice. It is clear that the graphs are used to compare the length of time needed to transmit cargo from Indonesia to Orlando, Florida through the title of the comparison. I believe it is longer because of the social issues like the pandemic causing many workers to stay home due to fear of getting sick. In general, many of the processes like the lead times and times needed to anchor in the seas have been extended likely due to the lack of staff. This affects me and my community because, with longer wait times, we'll have to wait longer for certain goods that we utilize on a daily basis. We might have to wait weeks or even months just for a single product we like from a specific company as a result of these delays. I believe that with this information I can come up with the headline "The Cargo Can't Wait to Travel! Or Maybe It's Waiting too Much?", which uses satire and humor in order to attract an audience to educate them on why shipments are taking longer than usual.

raw_comment:
1.  I noticed that transport times are taking longer than the typical amount of time it usually takes.

2. I wonder why cargo transit times are taking longer to arrive at the warehouses then usual

3. This graph affects me and my community because most of the products we get are shipped whether it'd be directly to your house or shipped to a facility or warehouse to be sold in a store.

4. This graph shows us the statistics for delayed cargo transit times as compared to the time it usually takes as a result of bottlenecking. "Supply chain bottlenecked?"

5. The reveal clarified to me that Covid isnt the sole reason for this supply chain disruption. Rather, companies are creating this bottleneck because of the inflation and shortage of products.

   Side-by-side **stacked vertical bar chart** (timeline-style comparison of transit times).

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **stacking** within each vertical bar to show component durations.
   - Uses a **side-by-side comparison** of two bars: “Typically 59 days” vs. “Currently 87 days.”
   - Includes **annotation callouts** and **icons** to explain delays and transportation modes.
   - No faceting or small multiples beyond the two compared bars.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Scenario (“Typically” vs. “Currently”) | Categorical/nominal | Separate side-by-side bars; top labels |
| Total transit time (days) | Quantitative | Overall bar height; top text labels (“59 days”, “87 days”) |
| Transit stage duration (days for each segment) | Quantitative | Height of stacked bar segments; numeric labels inside segments |
| Transit stage / shipment milestone (e.g., cargo ready to depart Indonesia, arrival in Vancouver, arrival in Ferndale, arrival in Orlando) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical position of orange milestone dots; text labels/callouts |
| Transportation mode | Categorical/nominal | Icons (factory/ship/rail/truck) placed alongside the bar; associated segment position |
| Delay explanation / cause | Categorical/nominal (textual annotation) | Annotation text connected by dotted leader lines |
| Sequence/order of shipment journey | Ordinal | Vertical ordering from top to bottom along the bars |

raw_comment:
I notice that there's a significant increase in the days that cargo is ready to depart from Indonesia & the transportation of goods by ship. There isn't a significant change in land delivery though. 

I wonder if Covid-19 has anything to do with the port congestion & capacity overflow. As for land deliveries, it's stated that wildfires are delaying the deliveries. I also wonder if other ports are having the same problems as what's happening in Vancouver. 

I don't really keep up with what's happening in the ports here in Hawaii but at my local Costco there has been quite a few shortages in certain items recently. 

Headline: As Covid-19 falls, more deliveries calls. 

New thought after the reveal: From the reveal I notice that Covid-19 isn't necessarily the reason for these bottlenecks but it's actually the shortage of parts for trikes. A delay of a single part for a certain item can cause a whole line of products to increase in price.

raw_comment: I noticed that transit time from Indonesia to Orlando is taking much longer than usual. It typically takes 59 days but due to lack of space in warehouses, it takes around 87 days. As time goes on, I wonder if the transit travel time will decrease because of the nearing end of the pandemic that caused for an increase in goods bought online. It relates to me and my community because my family as well as my neighbors have been buying many items online and the increase in travel time could interfere heavily with the influx of packages. A catchy headline would be: "Why Your Packages Are Always Late!"

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that compared to the typical cargo transit times from Indonesia to Orlando, Florida, the current transit times are much slower and extended in each phase. The biggest extension was in the travel time across the water where the typical time took 38 days and the current one takes 53 days, almost the entire length of travel for the typical cargo transit.
2. I wonder if this is due to the influx in supply and demand or the lack of workers in the chain. Did the Covid-19 precautions cause slower response times?
3. Shipping times for many products at the supermarket were delayed; therefore, many products were out of stock. This caused panic and hysteria and caused people to hoard items. In the early days of the pandemic it was hard for my family to get toilet paper, water, and other necessities.
4. One catchy headline for this graph can be "Shipping? More like Ship-Not." This catches the readers attention and the current issue on shipping.

raw_comment:
1.I notice that the supply chain delays have become more prevalent throughout the pandemic. Processes that would typically take around 59 days was now taking roughly three months. The pandemic slowed most businesses down, and now its beginning to seem like it was a permanent effect. 
2.I wonder how companies that rely on fast paced shipping plan to innovate their way past these heavy effects of the pandemic such as Amazon, and do these delays come as a result of people not working due to the Covid-19 Pandemic?
3. Longer these supplies take, jobs are at risk. People could get fired, and people could go into desperate states due to lack of supplies. Not many consumers are able to purchase what they need due to it being stranded in a warehouse in the middle of neverland; thus also affecting businesses due to lack of money flowing leading to them possibly closing down
4."Stuck at sea, my package never arrived to me!"

1. **Chart type**:  
   Side-by-side **stacked vertical bar chart** (timeline-style comparison of transit times).

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **stacking** within each vertical bar to show component durations.
   - Uses a **side-by-side comparison** of two bars: “Typically 59 days” vs. “Currently 87 days.”
   - Includes **annotation callouts** and **icons** to explain delays and transportation modes.
   - No faceting or small multiples beyond the two compared bars.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Scenario (“Typically” vs. “Currently”) | Categorical/nominal | Separate side-by-side bars; top labels |

| Transit stage duration (days for each segment) | Quantitative | Height of stacked bar segments; numeric labels inside segments |
| Transit stage / shipment milestone (e.g., cargo ready to depart Indonesia, arrival in Vancouver, arrival in Ferndale, arrival in Orlando) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical position of orange milestone dots; text labels/callouts |
| Transportation mode | Categorical/nominal | Icons (factory/ship/rail/truck) placed alongside the bar; associated segment position |
| Delay explanation / cause | Categorical/nominal (textual annotation) | Annotation text connected by dotted leader lines |
| Sequence/order of shipment journey | Ordinal | Vertical ordering from top to bottom along the bars |

4. An appropriate title for this graph would be “Where are your packages?”

raw_comment: I noticed right away the drastic difference in length between the two flow charts showing cargo transit times. I also noticed that the length of the transportation mode of the current transit time is 53 days, almost as long as the 59 days typical transit time total. Cargo also currently departs Indonesia 10 days later than it typically does as a result of capacity limits. I wonder if the cargo transit times are ever going to decrease again, or if this is the new normal. To follow up, I wonder if transit times will just continue to increase, especially considering the COVID-19 pandemic likely plays a role in the increased times. This relates to me and my community because packages are delivered much later not only to my family, but friends as well. For example, my sister had ordered fairy wings for Halloween, and they did not come in time. She had asked her friends if theirs did, and their wings were also delayed. I also saw many people complaining on TikTok that parts of their costumes were delayed, so it seems to be a common issue affecting many people. Based on this, a catchy title for this graph could be, "Increased Transit Times Resulting in Consumer Delivery Delays".

raw_comment:
I noticed that there was an increase in delays within all areas of transportation, however the longest delay was the transportation mode. Additionally, I noticed that there has been about a 50% increase in total wait time.

I wonder if transportation times would be quicker if it was shipped from Indonesia directly to Florida? What’s causing the warehouses to be full? Has this always been a problem? Is the labor shortage adding to this problem? 

This relates to me and my community because we all rely on shipping in order to get the supplies that we need. As we have become more and more dependent on shipping, out of stock and unavailable items are affecting our lives.

This graph depicts the wait times for shipping from Indonesia to Florida and explains why items are out of stock/unavailable. A catchy headline I came up with was “ Shipment Delays Cause Dismay”.

raw_comment:
1. I noticed in the graph that the cargo took 28 more days to deliver to arrive at Orlando, Florida. This significant because in theory, it could cause almost a month in delay for the shipping to arrive to consumers. 
2. This graph has made me wonder what other products are being delayed this long and what would be the cause of it. The graph mentions port congestion, and terminal digestion stemming from local deliveries in Vancouver. My question is that how and why are these problems occuring. One guess is that since quarantine, the demand has been unusually high and has created more demand for these products as shown by the trike (three-wheeled vehicles). If that is the problem, then I think the best option may be to wait out the pandemic until most people have been vaccinated, and hopefully things will go back to normal as it was before. Huge delays like the one shown in the graph is very problematic and indeed does disrupt the entire global trade. 
3. The graph shown and the delay time hasn't affected my community in significant ways. I did notice, however, a slight delay in Amazon delivery and I'm not too sure if it is also a result of the graph. One things I do know for sure, is that if this is a serious issue about bottleneck disruption, then it will most likely affect my community in the near future. 
4."A huge delay on good? What could this mean? -  I think this would be a fitting title as it asks questions about a mysterious problem that a person might not hear about

raw_comment:
1.  I noticed the significant difference between the two sides. A process that would typically take around 59 days was now taking around 87, due to congestion in ports, factories, railways, and more.
2.  The chart leads me to wonder if congestion was caused by the pandemic as many people began ordering many things online and caused a lot of problems in the workforce. 
3. This connects with my community because I as well as others have been ordering a lot of items online. Especially during the pandemic, people have become more reliant on ordering online; consequently, they are contributing to cargo delays. 
4. "Where is Your Package?"

| Sequence/order of shipment journey | Ordinal | Vertical ordering from top to bottom along the bars |

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   Side-by-side **stacked vertical bar chart** (timeline-style comparison of transit times).

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **stacking** within each vertical bar to show component durations.
   - Uses a **side-by-side comparison** of two bars: “Typically 59 days” vs. “Currently 87 days.”
   - Includes **annotation callouts** and **icons** to explain delays and transportation modes.
   - No faceting or small multiples beyond the two compared bars.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Scenario (“Typically” vs. “Currently”) | Categorical/nominal | Separate side-by-side bars; top labels |
| Total transit time (days) | Quantitative | Overall bar height; top text labels (“59 days”, “87 days”) |
| Transit stage duration (days for each segment) | Quantitative | Height of stacked bar segments; numeric labels inside segments |
| Transit stage / shipment milestone (e.g., cargo ready to depart Indonesia, arrival in Vancouver, arrival in Ferndale, arrival in Orlando) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical position of orange milestone dots; text labels/callouts |
| Transportation mode | Categorical/nominal | Icons (factory/ship/rail/truck) placed alongside the bar; associated segment position |
| Delay explanation / cause | Categorical/nominal (textual annotation) | Annotation text connected by dotted leader lines |
| Sequence/order of shipment journey | Ordinal | Vertical ordering from top to bottom along the bars |
raw_comment:
What do I notice:
First, I really like the visual appeal of the graphic. It is extremely innovative and original. It is also important to note that as of now, it takes 28 days longer to receive goods in Orlando from Indonesia than it usually does. It takes an extra 13 days for goods to be amassed in Indonesia. Surprisingly, shipping times from Vancouver to Washington has decreased by 2 days. 

What do I wonder? 
How much have these delays increased the price of goods due to, possibly, more expensive and lengthy delivery times.

raw_comment:
1,) I noticed that during this time frame although business itself has been slowly becoming steady again that the efficacy of transporting large shipments has decreased. Now, this can have multiple impacts on the communities and the people who are sending out and receiving these shipments.  
2.) I wonder how consumers are reacting to this problem and how the CEOs of these companies will fix it and help control an uprise if any. 
3.) In my community people have been feeling a delay with their orders especially once that is on the larger side such as furniture and this can cause some discomfort in our highly materialistic society.  
4.) Shipping overload would be the title that I would pick.

| Sequence/order of shipment journey | Ordinal | Vertical ordering from top to bottom along the bars |

raw_comment: I notice from the graph, that the time for the cargo to arrive in its final destination is taking 28 more days than it would typically. All the components of the process has increased by at least a couple of days, with the transportation part (I'm guessing cargo ships for international purposes) by 15 days. I wonder the reason for these delays is due partially to the pandemic and the shortage in workers in the shipping industry, specifically in the ports. Not only in ports, but warehouses who need people to work the equipment meant to transport cargo from certain places. This would lead to cargo just laying for days and create a backlog in the system, which would further delay the process with ships waiting and taking up space in the ports (port congestion). As a domino effect, the prices for spots on cargo ships would go up and sometimes the companies transporting them would be hesitant for fast service.

raw_comment:
1. I notice that these supply chain delays have become more prevalent during the pandemic. With the smaller capacity limits, the ships have to wait 10 days longer before they are able to depart. This delay causes a snowball effect, leading to more port congestion and other delays (ex. wildfires). This past year (and even currently), people have relied on online shopping to purchase a majority of their products, and the amount of goods purchased from stores has significantly increased. I'd assume that these factors have played a major role in the delays.

2. I wonder if this issue will get resolved, and how quickly. It seems like the rate of online shopping will continue to increase as we continue implementing technology and online services into our daily lifestyles, so I'm not sure if they'll have an opportunity to shut down the ports to reduce the port congestion. I am curious to see how this will play out in the future, and hope there will be a solution to these complications.

3. These delays are causing products to become unavailable to customers, which could include brands that my family uses regularly. While there are countless alternatives, it's just wild to think that products that have been in stores for decades on end have been unavailable recently.

4. Supply Chain Delays: A Global Trade Traffic Jam

raw_comment: This graph depicts the increase in cargo transit times from Indonesia to Orlando. The typical transit time of 59 days has increased to 87 days due to capacity limits, port congestion, terminal congestion, railway delivery delays, and full warehouses. My first question is when the first bar that shows a 59 day transit time is from. If it was pre-covid, that might give some explanation to the increase in transit time. If it was not from before covid, I wonder why the transit times have increased so much recently. I also wonder how these longer transit times are affecting things here in the US. This depends on what cargo is being imported. If we can't import raw materials fast enough, I think shortages in certain products could be likely since we can't manufacture them soon enough. My title for this graph is "Transit Delays: Why are they Increasing?"

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   Side-by-side **stacked vertical bar chart** (timeline-style comparison of transit times).

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **stacking** within each vertical bar to show component durations.

   - Includes **annotation callouts** and **icons** to explain delays and transportation modes.
   - No faceting or small multiples beyond the two compared bars.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Scenario (“Typically” vs. “Currently”) | Categorical/nominal | Separate side-by-side bars; top labels |
| Total transit time (days) | Quantitative | Overall bar height; top text labels (“59 days”, “87 days”) |
| Transit stage duration (days for each segment) | Quantitative | Height of stacked bar segments; numeric labels inside segments |
| Transit stage / shipment milestone (e.g., cargo ready to depart Indonesia, arrival in Vancouver, arrival in Ferndale, arrival in Orlando) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical position of orange milestone dots; text labels/callouts |
| Transportation mode | Categorical/nominal | Icons (factory/ship/rail/truck) placed alongside the bar; associated segment position |
| Delay explanation / cause | Categorical/nominal (textual annotation) | Annotation text connected by dotted leader lines |
| Sequence/order of shipment journey | Ordinal | Vertical ordering from top to bottom along the bars |

| Transportation mode | Categorical/nominal | Icons (factory/ship/rail/truck) placed alongside the bar; associated segment position |

| Sequence/order of shipment journey | Ordinal | Vertical ordering from top to bottom along the bars |

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that it takes a longer time for an good from Indonesia today than previously. 

2. I wonder if this is due to the pandemic, which leads to people preferring to have their goods delievered to them rather than them going outside to get the goods themselves. I also wonder how long ago "previously" is being used to define in this graph? Was it right before the pandemic, or actually sometime at the very beginning. The graph doesn't make that very clear. 
3. Nowadays, our community orders more stuff online. My family goes out to stores and restaurants less and less and order more take out and online deliveries when we want to buy or eat stuff.  

4. A good headline for this article could be "Cargo Shipping Experiences More Delays and Why".

   Side-by-side **stacked vertical bar chart** (timeline-style comparison of transit times).

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **stacking** within each vertical bar to show component durations.
   - Uses a **side-by-side comparison** of two bars: “Typically 59 days” vs. “Currently 87 days.”
   - Includes **annotation callouts** and **icons** to explain delays and transportation modes.
   - No faceting or small multiples beyond the two compared bars.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Scenario (“Typically” vs. “Currently”) | Categorical/nominal | Separate side-by-side bars; top labels |
| Total transit time (days) | Quantitative | Overall bar height; top text labels (“59 days”, “87 days”) |
| Transit stage duration (days for each segment) | Quantitative | Height of stacked bar segments; numeric labels inside segments |
| Transit stage / shipment milestone (e.g., cargo ready to depart Indonesia, arrival in Vancouver, arrival in Ferndale, arrival in Orlando) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical position of orange milestone dots; text labels/callouts |
| Transportation mode | Categorical/nominal | Icons (factory/ship/rail/truck) placed alongside the bar; associated segment position |
| Delay explanation / cause | Categorical/nominal (textual annotation) | Annotation text connected by dotted leader lines |
| Sequence/order of shipment journey | Ordinal | Vertical ordering from top to bottom along the bars |

raw_comment:
I noticed a significant change in the average transit time. It takes an average of 59 days to travel from Indonesia to Orlando. However, if we take a look at today, there is an 18-day difference. I've also noticed that shipping takes longer and finding warehousing space is more difficult. I'm curious as to why it takes so long to transport the products on the same routes but they arrive at different times. 
A good headline for this graph could be: Cargo Transit Time: The New Spiel

raw_comment:
1. I notice the already lengthy typical transit time has been drastically elongated by 28 days due to periodic delays.  From Indonesia to Vancouver, there is port congestion with ships and later on in the transit process, delays in railway deliveries because of wildfires. 
2. I wonder how long this delay in transportation will last, and if railway deliveries will be permanently affected by changes to the environment due to wildfires.

This can give people an insight into why they don’t receive their purchases as soon as expected. This also may explain a lack of stock in stores, as products cannot fit into warehouses and take longer to arrive in stores due to delays.
4. This graph shows the delayed transportation of cargo from Indonesia to Florida as a result of impediments throughout the transit process. A catchy headline might be: “Where’s my trike! Shipping delays?”

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that limits in the amount of products ships can hold is delaying lead times. Along with limited capacity, extra anchorage time also leads to delayed shipping and transport times, as it causes port congestion. For example, before arriving in Orlando it can take up to 60 days for the whole transport and departure process to take place. 
2. I wonder if the long and extra port congestion will have an impact on the environment of ports. Port waters are already filled with boats unloading cargo, and delayed departures from ports leads to more fuel and gas being deposited into the bodies of water around these ports. This not only pollutes the water but endangers aquatic life and the ecosystem of that body of water. 
3. This relates to me and my community because as global trade becomes more popular and easier, people are more likely to buy international goods. This means increased shipments and ships in port waters because of limited capacity and increased product demand. More ships in ports means a longer delay in ports and more pollution in the body of water. Many people demand fast shipping but don't realize the larger negative impacts it has on our environment. 
4. Title: "Snail Shipping"

raw_comment: This graph shows the increase in cargo transit times from Indonesia to Orlando, Fla. in recent days. Many Americans are facing a very large increase in the cost of goods but also a very large increase in the shipping time for goods. This is because, as shown in the graph, the cargo ports and warehouses are so congested from the surplus shipping of goods that it is putting a delay on all goods. I notice that typical transit times from Indonesia to Orlando, Fla. is 59 days, but now it takes 87 days. That is a huge increase in time for goods to ship and so I wonder what it is going to take to fix this. I also think that during the holiday season, this time is just going to continue to increase because now everyone has to buy gifts. I wonder when things are going to get better and if they are, how are people going to fix it.  The biggest reason for this is Coronavirus. This virus has changed every dynamic in the world. Everyone is ordering items online rather than going out to buy them because they don't need to be in contact with people online. This affects me and my community because I have experienced shipping delays in the past few months/year. I have ordered items online and when they normally ship in 1-2 weeks, they have shipped a month. This is affecting everyone in the world and I hope that it gets better soon. A catchy headline is, "Stuffed to the Brim".

1. What do you notice?
Storage capacity limits are skyrocketing because of more and more shopping online and the demand for products has increased over the past couple of years. Among human delays, wildfires and other natural disasters extend the time of transit for a product to reach its destination.
2. What do you wonder?
Is there an easier/faster solution to prevent congestion at transportation sites across the globe? If so what would it cost and is it within reach/feasible?

Holiday shopping shipping times have increased preventing gifts from reaching their destination before their hopeful arrival. I work at Target and the recent delays have increased working hours for most of the employees as more products are being purchased through the stores’ online distribution option. Before COVID the impact this had on staff was minimal but now that COVID has prevented some individuals from shopping inside the store the demand for online orders has increased exponentially.
4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.
People arent the alone in congestion...the global trade is too.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
The very first thing I notice is the header at the top of the graph distinguishing that the graph is discussing cargo transit times from Indonesia to Florida. After this, I make the connection that it takes a lot of time to make this journey when there are multiple stops taken. It can normally be a two day trip, but with the ships stopping in various places it takes ample more time. 
What do you wonder?
I have never seen this type of graph before and I wonder what it is called and what its main use is. I also wonder if there are people on the transit ships when they are making the additional stops. Is it cheaper to go on a ship that takes a longer period of time sort of like an airplane with layovers?
How does this relate to you and your community?
This does not directly relate to me and my community, but rather by an extension. These cargo ships are carrying items my household may have ordered, and with the additional stops it takes longer for my package to arrive. 
Create a headline. 
"Shipping...Shipping...Shipping... purchase your holiday items NOW"

raw_comment:
1.) I noticed that there is a drastic change in terms of the the typical transit time. More specifically, it typically takes 59 days to transit from Indonesia to Orlando. However, there is an 18 day difference if we were to fast forward to currently. This is due to the fact that capacity limits are creating longer lead times, along with extra anchorage time. Additionally, warehouses are full, so therefore its harder to encounter facilities with free space. Overall, the time to ship and transit has dramatically increased, leaving me with various questions along with concern. 
2.) I wonder what implications this might have on the American consumer population, especially with the holiday season right around the corner. I also wonder if this has any specific relation to Covid-19. Maybe overconsumption?
3.) In my community, most people shop online. On a daily basis, I think I see at least 20 delivery trucks pass my house, deliver packages to neighbors, or enter the main road. With shipping and transit times being consistently increased, this may breed frustration in my neighborhood, specifically because we are so reliant on online shopping. Not only in the online sense, my family as well as those who live around me shop a lot. I consistently see neighbors unloading bags of goodies, emphasizing the detrimental impact these delays have on my community. 
4.) Shipping delays? The Ultimate Pain!

raw_comment:

raw_comment: This graph showcases the supply chain delays that the supply and demand have caused. I believe it is comparing and contrasting two different cargo times traveling from Indonesia to Florida. One cargo time took 59 days to get to Florida and the other took 87 days. It took the second cargo an extra ten days to be ready to depart Indonesia. In addition, traveling time was an extra 15 days compared to the first cargo. Overall, many of the delays seem to be because there's too many goods for the current state of things like warehouses and ports. The supply was no ready for the amount of demand. I think a good name for the graph would be, "Cargo transit times vary in reponse to supply chain crisis"

Especially during the holiday season, this extra time that it is taking to get goods is very important to basically everyone ordering goods from different countries.

Holiday supply chain delays.

raw_comment:
The first thing I noticed about this graph was how long goods from Indonesia take to reach Vancouver and Orlando Florida. On the graph it says that some delays are stemming from Vancouver. I wonder what is causing these congestions and delays. Is it the pandemic? Low employment? One thing I also thought about was the climate and how long it may take boats trek across roaring seas in bad weather. 

Another thing I wonder is why it takes so long to get from Vancouver to Washington, when they are right next to each other. It might be an issue with crossing national borders though. Is the average time for a boat from Indonesia significantly lower than what is displayed on the graph? I would imagine that it would already take that long to go down the West Coast and through Central America. 

This affects me and my community because supply chain delays result in my purchased goods taking longer time to get to my house. 

Headline: How long does it take for your package to reach you?

raw_comment:
This graph shows that the cargo transit times from Indonesia to Orlando, Florida have become longer. I noticed that it now takes a longer time to ship goods from Indonesia to Orlando Florida. The transportation time for the goods had increased from 59 days to 87 days. This is due to port congestion, extra anchorage time and terminal congestion. The boat traveling time has increased from 38 days to 53 days.  Cargo preparation in Indonesia now takes 18 days while before it only took 8 days. I wonder what is causing these shipping delays.  I think it may be due to the shortage of workers in the shipping industries.  Also many deliveries are behind which is causing port congestion. I also wonder if the coronavirus pandemic affected the shipping deliveries. Are there less workers and delays in the shipping industry due to the coronavirus pandemic? This affects my community because my family and I often order stuff online from Amazon.  These shipping delays can cause the things that we ordered to get delayed. Also shipping delays can lead to a limit on products that I use everyday.  Stores may have low stock on items that I use from shipping delays. Also prices might increase due to less supply but more demand.  
Catchy Title = Shipping Delays and Why They Occur

raw_comment:
I notice that the Cargo transit time has increased from 59 days to 87 days. This is due to the capacity limits, port congestion, and warehouses being full. I wonder if this has to do with covid-19 or the high employment rates going on right now. Since everyone is home people might be ordering more and more stuff. This is relevant to me and my community because ordering things offline has become very common. The delay in transit time is inconvenient for everyone, but there is not anything we can do about it. 

“Why are your packages delayed”

1. What do you notice?

It is taking significantly longer for cargo to get from Indonesia to Florida. A whole extra 10 days in warehouses and 15 days in transportation!

2. What do you wonder?

Why is transportation taking so much longer? Like it says it's port congestion, but 15 days!

3. What impact does this have on you and your community?

Especially during the holiday season, this extra time that it is taking to get goods is very important to basically everyone ordering goods from different countries (cause this is definitely a worldwide problem, not just an Indonesia/ US problem) 

4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.

Holiday supply chain delays

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s flowchart shows the supply chain delays that are producing consumer goods and inventory shortages, long delivery delays and price increases -- inflation.   What factors contribute to these delays and how long will they affect inflation and the employment rate?  And, will you be getting a back-order slip in your Christmas stocking or as a holiday gift?

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to the four questions in the release.  By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included this graph and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, Nov. 19 with moderation on Wednesday, Dec. 1.  The topic:  global carbon displayed on a treemap graph.  Keep noticing and wondering!

I wonder: - If the difference for the number of days in manufacturing is because of a decrease in the amount of people working in factories? - If the reason that trucking is not delayed is because of the truck driver shortage? 

This relates to my community and I because we live in a digital age and in the midst of a pandemic so online shopping has becoming increasing popular amongst my community and I. 

"Are We There Yet"

raw_comment: After looking at the graph, I notice that it takes 28 more days than it typically does for cargo to get from Indonesia to Orlando. The transportation mode seems to be the biggest issue as there is a lot of port congestion. This means transportation which should only take 38 days is now taking 53 days. Something that came to mind that could cause delays is when the Suez Canal was obstructed by a container ship. I know that caused additional issues for cargo that had to get through that narrow space.

4. In this graph, bottlenecks are severely slowing down the process of transporting manufactured goods from country to country. A headline could be "Snail Mail!".

raw_comment:
1.) I notice that capacity limits are creating longer lead times which can lead to jam when it comes to transporting goods. For example, in the first row cargo can take up to 59 days to be delivered, 38 days being transportation, while in the second row cargo can take up to 287 days, 53 being transportation. 
2.)I wonder what the effects of this delay can have on the environment. The long days of transportation means longer use of vehicles and more pollution. Furthermore, I wonder what the environmental effects of these warehouses that are completely full. Are these warehouses the effect of increased consumerism? If so, is materialism becoming the norm in today's society? 
3.) This relates to my community since most people will take part in buying things from out of country which will lead to data similar to the ones displayed in the graph. Most consumers expect fast shipping without taking into account the effects they might have on the structure which provides for them altogether. 

Title: "What should I order next?"

raw_comment:
"Car go no go?"
(title translation - the cargo isn't going fast enough but also the cars aren't going fast enough)

I notice that it currently takes 87 days to deliver a package from Indonesia to Orlando. It typically only takes 59 days. I also notice that the package currently spends 18 days sitting around waiting to be delivered. It typically spends 8 days like this. I wonder how we could improve this in the future. It would make delivering cargo a lot better.
I notice that the cargo spends the most amount of time being delivered. It currently takes 87 days and should take 38. I happen to know that drivers have to sleep (you know, basic knowledge) and I wonder how much time could be saved if we used self driving trucks.

1. I notice that due to capacity limits creating longer lead times, as well as extra anchorage time happening because of port congestion, it takes over 39% longer for cargo to be transported from factories to ports in Vancouver, British Columbia. 
2. I wonder whether such disruptions in global trade have persisted throughout history, and are not only applicable to the current economy. It is possible that these bottlenecks originated due to a rapid and unforeseen increase in global trade as a result of emerging transportation technologies, increased manufacturing, and rapid globalization.
3. In my community, there is a shortage of several products due to bottlenecking. For example, most computers and smartwatches are out of stock due to bottlenecks in computer chip production and transportation, leading to higher demand.
4. In this graph, bottlenecks are severely slowing down the process of transporting manufactured goods from country to country.

raw_comment:
I notice that the largest time of increase was through the transportation through ship. The driving times don't get affected by much, however the warehouses are full because of the lack of cross country drivers.

I wonder if the blockage of the Suarez Canal has anything to do with the delay of products. I wonder if utilizing planes instead of ships would improve transport times. I wonder what the origin of the delays root from. I wonder if the times are most impacted from Indonesia or from all times.

This relates to my community because of Hawaii being so isolated, any products needed to get to Hawaii will take longer and longer until these shipping times get down. 

"SS: Slow Ships"

I notice that there is a significant increase in time for Cargo to be able to leave the port and when the cargo is in anchorage. Although the times for arrivals on land, the increases seem minor compared to the other delays in the shipping process.

In the process of the Cargo arrival to Ferndale, Wash, I observed the graph's fact that "railway deliveries have been delayed by wildfires". Another observation I made is that even warehouses, giant storage structures, are unable to withhold incoming supplies. Due to the drastic time increase of each delivery process, I question whether employees are working efficiently enough to "cure" the bottleneck situations. The delays in railroad shipments being connected to the growing number of forest fires in many communities proves citizens need to make greater efforts to save the ecosystem. Forest fires can dangerously affect the ecosystem; However, their also a contributing factor to supply shortages for many communities.

Title:
Dude, where's my car(go)?

I notice that the average time for transport from the two ports have increased by a large percentage. The most increase was the transportation via ship. The issue is further heightened by the issues with warehouse space. 

I wonder what caused the increase so much. could it be due to COVID-19. I also wonder how it is changed due to the new environmental regulations.

This connects to me because as a Hawaii resident things take a long time normally to ship due to an outdated law that restricts shipping, so this isn't helping me out.

raw_comment:
Holy SHIP! Why is my package taking forever?!

We noticed that, on average, it takes 28 more days to get a package from Indonesia to the US. According to the graph, the main reason for the congestion is at the ports in the US and Indonesia.

We wondered what underlying issues are causing this port congestion. We also wanted to know if there is a way to fix this problem.

This relates to our community because we are commonly consumers. As the holiday season rolls around, more people are ordering online to avoid crowds increasing shipping usage, further adding to the port congestion problem, prompting long wait times for commonly fast delivered packages.

raw_comment:
Q1. The biggest change is in the time for the cargo ready to leave Indonesia because it is over double the time. The biggest increase in days is with the transportation time with 15 days. The port congestion and carrying capacity seem to make life hard for those who need certain products. 
Q2. Why are warehouses at their capacities if it is taking forever to even transport it to them? What is it like to sit on a ship and wait to get into a port? How do these times and the changes to them compare to the times and changes of the airplanes? Are there any international products that take superiority over other products (like they get expedited somehow)?
Q3. In Hawaii, we are highly dependent on the shipment of products as we are an island nation and cannot produce many products. We can produce products that can be grown but manufactured products or products that need to go through factories and/or warehouses. When shipping to Hawaii, people often run into issues such as paying higher prices for postage and dealing with long delivery times. USPS is the only shipping carrier that treats shipping to Hawaii the same as shipping to any other state in the country. Since it costs extra money and time to ship things to Hawaii, the added time because of congestion and capacity limits will affect us heavily. Understanding bottlenecks are important to the supply and demand along with the inflation and deflation of prices in Hawaii. 
Q4. Title: Indonesia to Orlando but in 150% of the time.

raw_comment:
"Trips Around the World."

I notice that over a few years, the times increased by 28 days. Every step in the process had gained at least an extra day. The preparation time increased a lot. This could be due to a lack of materials or workers. The shipping time also increased by a good amount. This may have then led to an increase or delay in the steps that follow. 

I wonder why the prep. time is so long. Could this be from a small number of workers or a low amount of materials? Or something else? Also, if warehouses are full, why must they keep making more? Or are they full of different products?

   Side-by-side **stacked vertical bar chart** (timeline-style comparison of transit times).

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **stacking** within each vertical bar to show component durations.
   - Uses a **side-by-side comparison** of two bars: “Typically 59 days” vs. “Currently 87 days.”
   - Includes **annotation callouts** and **icons** to explain delays and transportation modes.
   - No faceting or small multiples beyond the two compared bars.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Scenario (“Typically” vs. “Currently”) | Categorical/nominal | Separate side-by-side bars; top labels |
| Total transit time (days) | Quantitative | Overall bar height; top text labels (“59 days”, “87 days”) |
| Transit stage duration (days for each segment) | Quantitative | Height of stacked bar segments; numeric labels inside segments |
| Transit stage / shipment milestone (e.g., cargo ready to depart Indonesia, arrival in Vancouver, arrival in Ferndale, arrival in Orlando) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical position of orange milestone dots; text labels/callouts |
| Transportation mode | Categorical/nominal | Icons (factory/ship/rail/truck) placed alongside the bar; associated segment position |
| Delay explanation / cause | Categorical/nominal (textual annotation) | Annotation text connected by dotted leader lines |
| Sequence/order of shipment journey | Ordinal | Vertical ordering from top to bottom along the bars |

raw_comment:
Title: "Where's That Package I Ordered 3 Months Ago?"

I notice that it takes a total of 28 extra days now than it used to to be able to transit cargo from Indonesia to Orlando, most of which are from the amount of time that it takes for the cargo to arrive by boat. I also notice that most of the reasons for delay are because of a lack of capacity in ships, ports, trains, warehouses, etc. All of these things have caused every process to take from 1 to 15 additional days. I wonder what causes the port conjunction in Vancouver, is it Covid related and is due to the number of people trying to find safer ways to purchase items or could it just be an uprise of companies using ships to transport their products? The same goes with the other modes of transportation and storage, why are all of the warehouses full these days compared to how they used to be? Could it also be because many businesses got affected by Covid-19 and are just now beginning to pick up the pace, therefore, causing more things to be produced and shipped out? Also, how does this affect the businesses that need these supplies? This could seriously affect the way a business is able to run and could even shut them down if they are not able to get the correct supplies for their products. The last thing that I wonder is if these wait times will ever reduce or if they will continue to grow and supply and demand changes in the future.

I notice that it is taking more time for the cargo to be transported. I also notice that the transportation is the longest part that has been extended. This is probably due to covid, and the holidays coming up soon. This could create to much cargo which would make the transportation of cargo much longer.

Everyone around the world has heard of this problem, and its still really bad. With cargo arriving late, many important things could be very late. This could include medical necessities, which is really bad because people in the hospital from things like the coronavirus, wont get what they need to survive.

raw_comment:
On this graph I notice multiple things, to start, I notice that 18 days longer to get the things than before. I also notice that the trucking capacity in Vancouver is far better than everywhere else. This could be due to the fewer restrictions in Canada.

Here are a few more things that I am noticing:
-------------------
-It jumped from 59 days to 87 days for transit between Indonesia and Orlando, Florida speed
-Longer anchorage time
-All of this creates a sort of domino effect because when one thing is slow, it slows the things that come after it.

I wonder if rebuilding some railways could be of help and I assume that the decrease in Coronavirus restrictions will assist in speeding things up.

A good title for this graph may be: Cargo, Let's Go!

raw_comment:
I noticed the drastic changes between the time it took for a cargo to arrive in Orlando. Port congestion has risen causing the days between delivery to rise drastically, but why has it risen? I wonder if its because of the pandemic causing demand of items to rise. While being at home for a year, people needed to find different way to safely buy items. The sudden change from a normal amount of orders to it multiplying in large could have been the reason delays have been so long. Other than waiting a little longer, I don't think this has caused much change for me and my community; however, it could have been hard for people to adjust to especially people not comfortable with electronics.
A title the graph could use is "How Bottlenecks are Delaying Cargo Transit Times"

raw_comment:
I noticed that the typical amount of time it took cargo to get to Orlando, Fla drastically changed, and there is a much longer amount of time that it takes currently. Usually, it would take 59 days, but currently, it takes 87 days. It took a lot of time to arrive in Vancouver, due to delays and extra anchorage time.
I wonder if this wouldn't be much of a problem if covid wasn't a thing. Covid has delayed so many things, so it is a big possibility that it has to do with the drastic changes. I also wonder why they have to put so much things on the cargo to go past the capacity limit. So, is there a lot of shortages happening? The last thing I wonder is if we are able to fix this. The changes are very sudden and huge, so it would be difficult to change this.
This relates to my community because we also have to get cargo and other stuff too. Due to covid, there has been a lot of shortages on food, and a lot of other essential supplies. If we don't have those, we could go down as a community with barely anything to live off of. The shortages have calmed don quite a bit, but it's still bad. People are more likely to get the virus if they aren't healthy, and they can't get healthy if all we have is delayed transportation for our essential needs.
In this graph, it is showing the changes in our cargo transportation, and showing why these changes are happening. Another good headline could be something along the lines of, "Drastic Changes in Cargo Transportation."

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
I notice that the capacity limits are creating longer lead times for packages. As well as this, there is extra anchorage time since there is port congestion and many warehouses are full to capacity so it is much harder to find facilities with space. The cargo transit times increased by more than one month. 
2. What do you wonder?
I wonder if this will change in the near future. I also wonder how the pandemic affected this global trade and how much money the actual price of goods increased. I also wonder if the transport of goods will decrease even more with the colder months quickly approaching since some oceans will be frozen and the cargo boats will have no place to go. 
3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
This impacts me and my community because since the holidays are coming up, this means that my family and I will have to order gifts more in advance if we want them to come in on time for the holidays. This could also mean that the prices of goods are increased so everything will be more expensive. 
4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.
In this graph, we see a flow chart of the cargo transit times from Indonesia to Orlando Florida, which increased from 59 days to 87 days. A catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea would be “How long will I have to wait for my order?”

raw_comment:
1.	I noticed that the speed of transportation from Indonesia to Orlando has increased due to various delays. Along with this, I noticed that compared to the typical transit times, the transportation modes have a much higher capacity limit. 
2.	I wonder what factor Covid plays in these delays that occur in transit. Along with this, I wonder if higher capacity limits have any impact on the speeds of the transit. 
3.	This relates to me and my community because it takes longer to deliver goods, so if you want to get something on time you have to order earlier. Along with this, goods are more expensive since there are higher demands due to the lack of supplies. 
4.	The graph is showing how the normal transit times between Indonesia and Orlando increased from 59 days to the current 87 days. Catchy headline: “Will I ever sea my package?”

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|

| Transportation mode | Categorical/nominal | Icons (factory/ship/rail/truck) placed alongside the bar; associated segment position |
| Delay explanation / cause | Categorical/nominal (textual annotation) | Annotation text connected by dotted leader lines |
| Sequence/order of shipment journey | Ordinal | Vertical ordering from top to bottom along the bars |

raw_comment:
We notice that there are delays in the current cargo transit from Indonesia to Orlando Florida. This is because there is a lot of congestion at the ports. There is a lot of supply but not enough demand for these product.

Both horizontal axis demonstrate this idea with the typical transit time and the actual transit time. There are labels with the number of days at certain points of the transportation. Something that is interesting is that global events affect congestion in ports, which in turn increases the time it takes for goods to be transported.

One thing we wonder is how the pandemic has affected this. Not only that, but we wonder if the ship that blocked the Suez canal had lasting effects that still effect the current time shown in this graph. One final aspect of this graph that we wonder about is whether the location of the destination and departure, Indonesia and Florida, affects certain factors like which canals the shipping container goes through, weather over the ocean, and the route that the ship takes.

raw_comment:
I noticed that all of the delays are caused by a monumental lack of storage for mainly ships and cargo. There is little space in both Indonesian and Canadian/American ports, causing a higher wait time for a ship's dockage. Also, the lack of warehouse space causes even more waiting. All of this adds up to cause a 28 day difference in cargo transit times from Indonesia to Orlando. 

I wonder why Orlando isn't generalized as "United States" or "Florida" like Indonesia is generalized. The city from which the ships left Indonesia isn't specified, but the city in which they arrive in the U.S. is specified. I also wonder why they chose specifically Indonesia to Orlando's ship trajectory and not any other cities. Maybe the sea route from Indonesia to Orlando is representative of all the delays and has the highest difference in transit time, or maybe the creators just chose a random city.

raw_comment:
I noticed that because of so many goods that are being transported there is a lot of congestion in the ports. There is such a high demand in the cargo transportation but also a lack of time and space. This is an overload or surplus of transportation with a lack of capacity and resources to pursue the cargo routes. 

I wonder what solution could be made to fix this. Will Orlando have to drop one of the transit lines temporarily?

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   Side-by-side **stacked vertical bar chart** (timeline-style comparison of transit times).

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **stacking** within each vertical bar to show component durations.
   - Uses a **side-by-side comparison** of two bars: “Typically 59 days” vs. “Currently 87 days.”
   - Includes **annotation callouts** and **icons** to explain delays and transportation modes.
   - No faceting or small multiples beyond the two compared bars.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Scenario (“Typically” vs. “Currently”) | Categorical/nominal | Separate side-by-side bars; top labels |
| Total transit time (days) | Quantitative | Overall bar height; top text labels (“59 days”, “87 days”) |
| Transit stage duration (days for each segment) | Quantitative | Height of stacked bar segments; numeric labels inside segments |
| Transit stage / shipment milestone (e.g., cargo ready to depart Indonesia, arrival in Vancouver, arrival in Ferndale, arrival in Orlando) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical position of orange milestone dots; text labels/callouts |
| Transportation mode | Categorical/nominal | Icons (factory/ship/rail/truck) placed alongside the bar; associated segment position |
| Delay explanation / cause | Categorical/nominal (textual annotation) | Annotation text connected by dotted leader lines |
| Sequence/order of shipment journey | Ordinal | Vertical ordering from top to bottom along the bars |
raw_comment:
I noticed that the graph is showing the process of items being transported from Indonesia to Orlando, Florida typically,  compared to currently. I noticed that the amount of time that it currently takes is much longer than the amount of time that it typically takes. In particular, the lead times was increased by 10 days because of capacity limits & anchorage time was increased by 15 days because of port congestions. 

I wonder why there are such major delays when transporting these goods & I wonder what is causing the port congestions. Is it caused by the pandemic? Do these longer Cargo Transit Times also increase the demand for items in Orlando, Florida?

This might relate to my community and I because the demand for certain supplies may increase because of the delays. This may change prices of items and cause inflation in the economy (long term.)

"28 More Days, How Much More $?"

Possible title: "Impacts of COVID-19 on supply chains and the supply and demand of Cargo From Indonesia"

Wonders?

How to companies that rely on fast paced shipping plan to innovate their way past these delays?

What economic effects do these delays have on the value and demand of these products?

Does a 26 day delay really make that much of a difference?

Do these delays have to do with the lack of people in the labor force due to covid-19?

It seems that the transportation method delays is the root of most of the delay.

Is this phenomenon applicable to cargo shipped from other places other than Indonesia?

raw_comment: I noticed that the cargo times from Indonesia to Orlando, Florida have increased by 28 days. Specifically the times from Indonesia to Vancouver, British Columbia significantly increased to 15 days. Additionally, getting the cargo ready to depart Indonesia increased by 10. I wonder how and why the capacity limits changed in Indonesia since it is impacting the lead times to be longer. Additionally, I wonder when porting congestion and extra anchorage started to occur because it has impacted the departure and arrival times to increase significantly. I wonder what they are doing to reduce the cargo transit times and resolve the issue like using planning, a better outsourcing model, and stronger scheduling. This relates to me and my community because there is an ongoing trend with economic outsourcing especially online. An abundance of people ranging from adolescents to adults order a lot of things online. While ordering online, there is a long delayment in shipping packages out and obtaining our deliveries. We figured out a portion of why sometimes things don't come in on time and why things outside the country take a long time to ship. The graph demonstrates how a larger population and increase in supply and demand impacts outsourcing in the cargo transit times from Indonesia to Orlando, Florida; additionally, it may impact future production and outsourcing which can cause distress. A catchy headline to wrap the main idea is, "Products Placed in Postponement!"

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   Side-by-side **stacked vertical bar chart** (timeline-style comparison of transit times).

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **stacking** within each vertical bar to show component durations.
   - Uses a **side-by-side comparison** of two bars: “Typically 59 days” vs. “Currently 87 days.”
   - Includes **annotation callouts** and **icons** to explain delays and transportation modes.
   - No faceting or small multiples beyond the two compared bars.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Scenario (“Typically” vs. “Currently”) | Categorical/nominal | Separate side-by-side bars; top labels |
| Total transit time (days) | Quantitative | Overall bar height; top text labels (“59 days”, “87 days”) |
| Transit stage duration (days for each segment) | Quantitative | Height of stacked bar segments; numeric labels inside segments |
| Transit stage / shipment milestone (e.g., cargo ready to depart Indonesia, arrival in Vancouver, arrival in Ferndale, arrival in Orlando) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical position of orange milestone dots; text labels/callouts |
| Transportation mode | Categorical/nominal | Icons (factory/ship/rail/truck) placed alongside the bar; associated segment position |
| Delay explanation / cause | Categorical/nominal (textual annotation) | Annotation text connected by dotted leader lines |
| Sequence/order of shipment journey | Ordinal | Vertical ordering from top to bottom along the bars |

   Side-by-side **stacked vertical bar chart** (timeline-style comparison of transit times).

   - Uses **stacking** within each vertical bar to show component durations.
   - Uses a **side-by-side comparison** of two bars: “Typically 59 days” vs. “Currently 87 days.”
   - Includes **annotation callouts** and **icons** to explain delays and transportation modes.
   - No faceting or small multiples beyond the two compared bars.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Scenario (“Typically” vs. “Currently”) | Categorical/nominal | Separate side-by-side bars; top labels |
| Total transit time (days) | Quantitative | Overall bar height; top text labels (“59 days”, “87 days”) |
| Transit stage duration (days for each segment) | Quantitative | Height of stacked bar segments; numeric labels inside segments |
| Transit stage / shipment milestone (e.g., cargo ready to depart Indonesia, arrival in Vancouver, arrival in Ferndale, arrival in Orlando) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical position of orange milestone dots; text labels/callouts |
| Transportation mode | Categorical/nominal | Icons (factory/ship/rail/truck) placed alongside the bar; associated segment position |
| Delay explanation / cause | Categorical/nominal (textual annotation) | Annotation text connected by dotted leader lines |
| Sequence/order of shipment journey | Ordinal | Vertical ordering from top to bottom along the bars |

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   Side-by-side **stacked vertical bar chart** (timeline-style comparison of transit times).

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **stacking** within each vertical bar to show component durations.
   - Uses a **side-by-side comparison** of two bars: “Typically 59 days” vs. “Currently 87 days.”
   - Includes **annotation callouts** and **icons** to explain delays and transportation modes.
   - No faceting or small multiples beyond the two compared bars.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Scenario (“Typically” vs. “Currently”) | Categorical/nominal | Separate side-by-side bars; top labels |
| Total transit time (days) | Quantitative | Overall bar height; top text labels (“59 days”, “87 days”) |
| Transit stage duration (days for each segment) | Quantitative | Height of stacked bar segments; numeric labels inside segments |
| Transit stage / shipment milestone (e.g., cargo ready to depart Indonesia, arrival in Vancouver, arrival in Ferndale, arrival in Orlando) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical position of orange milestone dots; text labels/callouts |
| Transportation mode | Categorical/nominal | Icons (factory/ship/rail/truck) placed alongside the bar; associated segment position |
| Delay explanation / cause | Categorical/nominal (textual annotation) | Annotation text connected by dotted leader lines |
| Sequence/order of shipment journey | Ordinal | Vertical ordering from top to bottom along the bars |
raw_comment:
Table #6: Juan, Lana

Something we noticed on this graph was that supplies took longer to arrive to Orland due to many stops and time constrains for the making of supplies. Also another factor being time, the more days that a delay occurs the more difficult it is to send supplies to their given destinations.

Something we wonder is what are possible causes for delays, given that railways, wildfires, and the pandemic being a key factor for many stops. We also wonder what are some of the effects for workers who transport supplies, how do they feel within these long delays and how do they go on within delivering supplies. 

This affects our community within the breakdown in fear that  supplies not arriving in time for jobs and for consumers. Longer these supplies take, jobs are at risk with these supplies making stops almost a month later than usual bringing the risk factor much higher.

Catch Headline: Where the Cargo at tho?

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Scenario (“Typically” vs. “Currently”) | Categorical/nominal | Separate side-by-side bars; top labels |
| Total transit time (days) | Quantitative | Overall bar height; top text labels (“59 days”, “87 days”) |

| Transit stage / shipment milestone (e.g., cargo ready to depart Indonesia, arrival in Vancouver, arrival in Ferndale, arrival in Orlando) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical position of orange milestone dots; text labels/callouts |
| Transportation mode | Categorical/nominal | Icons (factory/ship/rail/truck) placed alongside the bar; associated segment position |

| Sequence/order of shipment journey | Ordinal | Vertical ordering from top to bottom along the bars |

I notice that there has been a huge delay in the time it takes for cargo to arrive in Vancouver from Indonesia. This later affects the time it takes for the cargo to get to Ferndale, then Orlando.
What do I wonder?
I wonder if these delays are happening because of Covid or something else.
How does this relate to my community?
This relates to my community because it can affect our daily lives. Because of these delays some people may not be able to get certain goods that they need for example.
Headline
A headline I would use to describe this graph would be "Cargo transit times are getting longer and longer. Why?"

raw_comment:
I notice that the time to deliver products has increased by approximately 67.8% because of demand caused by the Covid-19 pandemic. As vaccination rates increase, and things are beginning to return to normal, people have began ordering products at an increased rate, overworking our shipping system that had been struggling beforehand. 
I wonder how this will effect our economy and how long it will take to get back to normal, and if the delta strain becomes an even more looming obstacle how that will continue to affect delivery.
This relates to my community because it has to do with how long it takes to receive sometimes necessary products, and putting some workers out of a job. It does force us to shop locally though.
My title would be: 
"Bottleneck trade, how will it effect us and our workers?"

|---|---|---|

| Sequence/order of shipment journey | Ordinal | Vertical ordering from top to bottom along the bars |

raw_comment:
It is a widely held belief that bottlenecks disrupt global trade and affect us all. 
To begin with, lots of delays are undoubtedly observed during cargo transit times and cause supply chain problems, which are really crucial. These delays may be results of misorganization, extra anchorage time or even wildfires. It goes without saying that these retardations may be proven extremely important and can impact negatively on our lives, relationships, habits, or even priorities.
In my opinion, should global trade be disrupted, we will all be deprived of food, medication and clothes, due to the undenible fact that our world operates through trade, imports and exports, as globalization is increased day by day.
I am inclined to think that global trade is an integral part of our lives and existence, as the fact of realizing that we, people, cannot do without it is really vital.
